title: Translating CUDA Tile Operations from Python to Rust Using Agentic AI | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA built a bounded multi-agent skill that translated all 24 public TileGym operators (~40 kernels) from cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR into cuTile Rust at 0.995 geomean parity on DGX B200, at about half the token cost, with every stage gated by machine-checkable verdicts and Tile IR structural diffing. The deeper claims are that a shared cuda_tile IR makes front-end choice performance-neutral and verifiable, and that a pure-routing orchestrator with artifact-only subagent communication is what makes 24 unattended conversions repeatable rather than lucky.

insights.claim: An AI agent skill ported all 24 public TileGym operators, roughly 40 GPU kernels spanning element-wise ops through flash-attention decode, Multi-head Latent Attention, and mixture-of-experts, from cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR into cuTile Rust at 99.5% of cuTile Python performance on average.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Demonstrates agents doing production compiler-adjacent engineering at parity, not toy code generation, which is the strongest available evidence for agentic coding ROI.
insights.quote: we ported all 24 public TileGym operators to cuTile Rust and reached 99.5% of cuTile Python performance on average.

insights.claim: Benchmarking with CUPTI device time on NVIDIA DGX B200 across 347 paired configurations covering the 24 operators produced an overall geomean of 0.995 versus cuTile Python, with all 24 operators clearing the 0.95 threshold and about a third beating the reference.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Statistically broad parity, not cherry-picked wins, makes the language migration effectively free in performance terms.
insights.quote: Overall geomean is 0.995, parity with cuTile Python.

insights.claim: Using the skill cut token cost to about half on average per conversion while validating every operator for numerical correctness and a geomean speedup of at least 0.95.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Token economics are the real constraint on agentic engineering, so halving cost per task is what turns a demo into a batch production pipeline.
insights.quote: Token cost drops to about half on average, every operator is validated for numerical correctness, and each one hits a geomean speedup of ≥0.95 versus cuTile Python.

insights.claim: A full kernel conversion runs on the order of millions of tokens, which is one of the two explicit reasons the work is split across specialized subagents rather than handled in a single context.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Million-token task budgets set a hard floor on inference demand for agentic software engineering and explain why context economy drives architecture.
insights.quote: First, a full conversion runs on the order of millions of tokens.
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

themes.theme: Shared IR as the verification substrate

insights.claim: cuTile Python, Triton-TileIR, and cuTile Rust are three front ends over the same CUDA Tile IR cuda_tile dialect, all feeding the same tileiras compiler that performs tile-level optimization and emits the GPU binary.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: A converged IR under multiple DSLs is NVIDIA's answer to Triton fragmentation and the structural reason a language port can be performance-neutral.
insights.quote: cuTile Python, Triton-TileIR, and cuTile Rust are three front ends over the same IR: CUDA Tile IR, the cuda_tile dialect.
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: Because all three front ends meet at the same IR, porting a kernel is re-expressing the same tile program in a safer host language with the same compiler and performance model underneath, not a re-optimization problem.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Reframes language migration cost: when the optimizer is shared, the front end becomes a developer-experience choice rather than a performance bet.
insights.quote: porting a kernel to cuTile Rust is not a re-optimization problem. It is re-expressing the same tile program in a safer host language, with the same compiler and the same performance model underneath.
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: A faithful port can be checked structurally by dumping and diffing the reference and translated Tile IR before a single test runs, verifying the same memory-op families, tile shapes, and reductions.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Structural verification ahead of functional testing is a generalizable recipe for trusting agent output in any domain with a canonical intermediate representation.
insights.quote: this can be directly verified by dumping the reference kernel Tile IR and the translated kernel Tile IR and “diffing” them before a single test is executed.
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: Functional tests alone are insufficient because a wrong-but-plausible translation, such as a TMA load with the wrong cost hint or a dropped divisibility attribute, can pass tests yet be incorrect outside test coverage and cause performance regressions.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: The central risk of AI-generated systems code is plausible-but-wrong output that passes CI, which argues for structural checks over test coverage alone.
insights.quote: A wrong-but-plausible translation (a TMA load with wrong cost hint or a dropped divisibility attribute, for example) can pass tests yet still be incorrect outside of test coverage
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: The shared cuda_tile dialect makes IR diffing the backbone of verification at two points, as the kernel writer's self-check before tests run and as the IR-diff analyst's deep comparison on failure, rejecting structurally wrong translations such as a reduction on the wrong axis or a lost mask.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Two-stage structural gating is why 24 unattended conversions were repeatable rather than lucky, a pattern any agentic code pipeline can copy.
insights.quote: rejecting structurally wrong translations (a reduction on the wrong axis, a lost mask) that would otherwise pass as plausible.
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

insights.claim: Since experiments capture only device time, the authors expect that matching the emitted Tile IR exactly would match performance exactly across front ends, though kernels written that way become uninterpretable, so the skill is deliberately biased toward idiomatic code.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: An explicit readability-versus-exact-parity tradeoff: the last 0.5% of performance is available but costs maintainability.
insights.quote: we expect that matching the emitted Tile IR exactly would match performance exactly across front ends.

insights.claim: The main translation challenge is that cuTile Python JIT compilation specializes each kernel implicitly at call time while Rust requires every specialization to be declared in the kernel's signature.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Names the precise semantic gap that makes Python-to-systems-language ports hard, and why an agent plus a rulebook beats naive transpilation.
insights.quote: The main challenge is that cuTile Python JIT compilation specializes each kernel implicitly at call time, whereas Rust requires that you declare every specialization in the kernel’s signature.

insights.claim: In cuTile Rust the GPU binary is still JIT-compiled at first launch from an embedded kernel AST with concrete const-generic values and cached thereafter, but the implicitness is gone because nothing is specialized unless the signature declares it.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Ahead-of-time type checking with late binary specialization is a hybrid model that keeps JIT flexibility while making constraints machine-checkable.
insights.quote: The GPU binary itself is still JIT-compiled, but the implicitness is gone: nothing is specialized unless the kernel signature declares it.
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: Dropped branches in Python force structural splitting in Rust, so one Python kernel becomes multiple Rust entries, for example layer_norm splitting into 2-D nchw and 1-D w1 entries because the branch changes tile rank.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Kernel count inflation is a hidden maintenance cost of moving to a statically typed GPU DSL that raw performance benchmarks do not show.
insights.quote: One Python kernel becomes multiple structural Rust entries (for example, layer_norm splits into 2-D nchw and 1-D w1 entries because the branch changes tile rank)
insights.locator: Table 1, Examples of cuTile Python-Rust translation gaps

insights.claim: Where Python compiles any dtype combination on demand, the Rust FFI dispatches over a fixed symbol and dtype table spanning f32/f16/bf16/i32/i64/f8e5m2/f8e4m3fn, making each new dtype an explicit ABI extension.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Static dispatch tables trade flexibility for auditability, and the enumerated FP8 variants show where low-precision formats have become table stakes.
insights.quote: Supporting a dtype is an explicit ABI extension; the shared table spans f32/f16/bf16/i32/i64/f8e5m2/f8e4m3fn
insights.locator: Table 1, Examples of cuTile Python-Rust translation gaps

insights.claim: Past the C ABI there is no safety net, so a wrong stride becomes silent corruption rather than an exception, which is why the design adds two defensive layers of semantic checks in the Python wrapper and ABI checks for null, dtype, and device behind the FFI with named return codes.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: The safety story of Rust kernels stops at the FFI boundary, a nuance that tempers the marketing claim of safe GPU programming.
insights.quote: Past the C ABI there is no safety net, so a wrong stride is a silent corruption, not an exception
insights.locator: Table 1, Examples of cuTile Python-Rust translation gaps

insights.claim: The softmax example shows what Python leaves implicit becoming an explicit type in Rust, with every intermediate typed as a Tile<f32, {[1, TILE_SIZE]}> and a keepdims=True reduction expanding into a reduce_* call followed by explicit reshape and broadcast.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Verbosity is the concrete price of static safety in GPU DSLs, which is exactly the tedium an agent can absorb.
insights.quote: What cuTile Python keeps implicit becomes an explicit type.

themes.theme: Rust ownership applied to GPU kernels

insights.claim: cuTile Rust extends the Rust ownership model to tile-based GPU kernels by splitting mutable outputs into disjoint pieces and preserving the host-side ownership contract across kernel launches, while allowing local opt-out for direct Tile IR execution.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Bringing memory-safety guarantees into GPU kernel authoring is a genuine language-level shift that could reshape who can write performant CUDA code.
insights.quote: Extending the Rust ownership model to tile-based GPU kernels, it splits mutable outputs into disjoint pieces and preserves the host-side ownership contract across kernel launches.

insights.claim: The FFI launcher never copies, never allocates, and never takes ownership, wrapping the PyTorch device pointer in a ManuallyDrop<Tensor> so Rust hands the kernel its tensors without ever freeing memory it does not own, and launching asynchronously on the caller's CUDA stream.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Zero-copy, zero-allocation interop is what lets a Rust kernel backend drop into PyTorch pipelines without performance or lifetime hazards.
insights.quote: the launcher never copies, never allocates, and never takes ownership.

insights.claim: Not all shipped TileGym kernels use the fully safe style yet, because each port must reproduce the reference kernel Tile IR exactly and where only an unchecked API reproduces it the port uses that API, with migration onto the safe surface still underway.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: A candid admission that IR fidelity currently outranks safety, so the safe-Rust-GPU pitch is aspirational for part of the library today.
insights.quote: Note that not all of the shipped kernels in TileGym use this fully safe style yet.

insights.claim: cuTile Rust is exposed as just another TileGym backend selectable with tilegym.set_backend("cutile-rs"), routing the same operator API to the Rust kernels.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Backend-swappable architecture means users can adopt Rust kernels without changing call sites, removing the usual migration blocker.
insights.quote: in TileGym, cuTile Rust is simply another backend. tilegym.set_backend("cutile-rs") routes the same operator API to the Rust kernels.
insights.locator: Kernel translation between Tile IR front ends

insights.claim: The Rust backend compiles lazily by tracking source freshness, so editing any kernel.rs or the crate manifest makes the next call rebuild the shared library before dispatch with no explicit cargo build in the develop-test cycle.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Removing the compile step from the inner loop closes the iteration-speed gap that normally keeps kernel authors in Python.
insights.quote: Iterating on a tile kernel in Rust is as easy as it is in Python: change the kernel, run the test, and the new binary is already in place.

themes.theme: Multi-agent pipeline design: orchestrator does no work

insights.claim: The skill is built around the design decision that the agent loading it does no engineering work at all, becoming a pure orchestrator whose only authority is routing while specialized subagents each load only the reference documents their stage needs.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Separating routing authority from execution authority is the reusable architectural insight, applicable far beyond kernel translation.
insights.quote: the agent that loads it does no engineering work at all. Reading SKILL.md turns the top-level agent into a pure orchestrator whose only authority is routing
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

insights.claim: Subagents communicate only through artifacts with fixed schemas and never through conversation, each stage ends in a machine-checkable verdict the orchestrator routes on without reading prose, and nothing in the loop depends on one LLM interpreting another LLM's prose.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Eliminating LLM-to-LLM prose interpretation is presented as the specific mechanism converting luck into repeatability, a testable claim for anyone building agent systems.
insights.quote: Nothing in the loop depends on one LLM interpreting the prose of another LLM. This is what makes 24 unattended conversions repeatable rather than lucky.

insights.claim: The kernel writer subagent is barred from touching host code so its failures stay attributable, and it proves its work twice: functionally via an in-Rust pipeline test with no FFI and no Python so a numerics bug cannot hide behind host plumbing, and structurally via an IR self-check.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Blame isolation by scope restriction is how you keep multi-agent retries cheap, a direct answer to the debugging problem in agent pipelines.
insights.quote: Barred from host code, its failures stay attributable.
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

insights.claim: The analyzer subagent solves the JIT-hides-the-spec problem by benchmarking the operator's cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR implementations, selecting the faster one per structural variant as the reference, dumping its Tile IR, and writing analysis.json with variants, constants, dtypes, tolerances, launch grids, autotune space, and the chosen baseline.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Materializing an implicit spec into a machine-readable artifact is the step that makes every downstream agent decision checkable.
insights.quote: it dumps the Tile IR of that reference for each variant (the ground truth for the kernel writer) and writes analysis.json
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

insights.claim: The performance validator runs a CUPTI benchmark protocol with device-time measurement and per-config pairing against the reference on the same GPU, requiring the geometric mean to land within 5% of the reference, and its job is explicitly to measure honestly rather than optimize.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Separating the measure role from the optimize role removes the incentive to tune a benchmark, a governance pattern worth copying.
insights.quote: Its job is not to optimize but to measure honestly.
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

insights.claim: Two diagnostic specialists join only on failure and neither edits code: the IR-diff analyst classifies divergences and crucially separates a mistranslation from an upstream compiler bug that no kernel change can fix, while the residual-performance investigator root-causes slow-but-correct kernels on both device and host sides.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Distinguishing agent error from tool error is the failure mode that silently burns retry budget in most agent systems.
insights.quote: this separates a mistranslation (route back to the kernel writer with a specific fix) from an upstream compiler bug that no kernel change can fix.
insights.locator: How does the agent skill work?

themes.theme: Bounded control loop and production driver

insights.claim: Every subagent return must end with a literal <VALIDATOR_OUTPUT> block and one VERDICT line, the orchestrator checks exit codes then routes purely on the verdict, and a malformed return earns exactly one same-agent repair respawn and never an escalation.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Hard output contracts plus a one-shot repair rule are how you stop agent loops from degrading into unbounded retry spirals.
insights.quote: Every subagent return must end with a literal <VALIDATOR_OUTPUT> block and one VERDICT: line.

insights.claim: Hard spawn caps bound the run at one analysis, two kernel-writer and two host-builder attempts, one diagnosis, two benchmark runs, and one optional perf pass, so a run either converges within budget or stops with a diagnosis on disk and cannot thrash.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Explicit attempt budgets turn unbounded agent cost into a predictable line item, which is what makes batch agentic engineering financeable.
insights.quote: A run either converges within the budget or stops with a diagnosis on disk; it cannot thrash.

insights.claim: A missing owner tag on a failure route is itself treated as a failure and the orchestrator stops rather than guessing, because a host fault misrouted to the kernel stage wastes an entire retry.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Fail-stop on ambiguous routing is a cost-driven design choice, showing retry budget as the scarce resource in agent systems.
insights.quote: A missing owner tag is itself a failure. The orchestrator stops rather than guessing because a host fault misrouted to the kernel stage wastes an entire retry.

insights.claim: A preflight script verifies environment variables and toolchain paths before anything spawns, on the reasoning that a non-zero exit means the environment is unusable and no amount of agent effort fixes a missing compiler.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Cheap deterministic environment checks before expensive model calls is basic but frequently skipped agent-pipeline hygiene.
insights.quote: the environment is unusable, and no amount of agent effort fixes a missing compiler.

insights.claim: The skill's 49 coding rules are a distilled failure history in which each rule exists because an early conversion produced a kernel that compiled but was wrong without it, ranging from narrow constraints like assume_div_by applying only to pointers to structural ones like a broadcast must be preceded by a reshape.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Encoding accumulated failure modes as explicit rules is how agent skills compound in value, and it is a durable asset a competitor cannot copy quickly.
insights.quote: Each one exists because an early conversion produced a kernel that compiled but was wrong without it.

insights.claim: In production a one-shot driver creates a fresh checkout on a per-operator branch, hides any pre-existing implementation of the target operator so the agent must actually translate, launches the agent in a detached container, polls progress from outside, and autocommits only on a green acceptance check.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Hiding the answer to prevent the agent from cheating is a leakage control that benchmark-conscious readers should demand of any agentic coding claim.
insights.quote: hides any pre-existing implementation of the target operator (so the agent must translate), launches the agent in a container detached from the operator’s terminal

insights.claim: The acceptance check requires three simultaneous conditions: TileGym correctness green, proof that the cuTile Rust backend actually executed, and a CUPTI geomean speedup of at least 0.95 against the cuTile Python baseline, with a batch driver allowing at most two attempts per operator.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: A three-part gate including proof-of-execution guards against the classic agent failure of silently falling back to the old implementation.
insights.quote: TileGym correctness is green, proof that the cuTile Rust backend actually executed, and CUPTI geomean speedup ≥ 0.95 against the cuTile Python baseline.

insights.claim: Each conversion lands as a standard six-file changeset and the final aggregate rechecks a 17-file output contract across all stages covering reports, IR dumps, correctness, and performance logs, so human review stays mechanical.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Standardized artifact shape is what keeps human review cost flat as agent output volume scales, the practical limit on agentic engineering throughput.
insights.quote: Each conversion lands as a standard six-file changeset, so review stays mechanical.

insights.claim: The skill and all converted operators ship publicly in the NVIDIA/TileGym GitHub repo under skills/tilegym-converting-python-to-rust/, including per-stage agent instructions, a coding rulebook, concept guides, validator scripts, and fully worked softmax and bmm examples.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the agent skill itself, not just the output, is a distribution play that normalizes NVIDIA's IR and DSL as the substrate for AI-written kernels.
insights.quote: Access the skill through skills/tilegym-converting-python-to-rust/.
insights.locator: Get started with cuTile Rust agent skills

insights.claim: Running the pipeline requires CUDA 13.1 or newer, a Blackwell GPU for the performance check, Rust 1.89 or newer, and the tileiras compiler.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: A Blackwell requirement gates the workflow to current-generation NVIDIA hardware, converting a developer-tooling story into hardware pull-through.
insights.quote: Requirements: CUDA 13.1+, a Blackwell GPU for the perf check, Rust 1.89+, and the tileiras compiler.
insights.locator: Get started with cuTile Rust agent skills

insights.claim: The runtime activates the skill by matching a task description rather than an explicit invocation, so a user can point any agent at the repo and ask it to add a cutile-rs backend for an operator and the pipeline handles analysis, kernel, FFI, correctness, and benchmarking.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: Description-matched skill activation points toward a future where library vendors ship agent capabilities alongside APIs, and discoverability becomes a distribution channel.
insights.quote: To get started, point any agent at the repo and ask it to “add a cutile-rs backend for <op>“.
insights.locator: Get started with cuTile Rust agent skills

insights.claim: Wall-clock and device time are treated as answering different questions on submicrosecond kernels, so the team measures wall clock but reports CUPTI device time to keep operator-to-operator comparison about the kernels rather than launch and scheduling overhead.
insights.speaker: Yinuo Liu
insights.so_what: The reported parity excludes launch overhead, so end-user wall-clock experience of the Rust backend is not what the headline 0.995 measures.
insights.quote: Wall-clock time includes launch and scheduling cost and reflects what the user experiences, while CUPTI device time compares the kernels in isolation.
